title: The yogis on the mountain
hook: Himalayan yogis ask why he stays in the world; he answers that you live in it without being stained

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hand on the rock at Hasan Abdal. Your line was a steady hand. When something came at you, did your hand stay open? Day thirty-nine.

There's a fantasy most of us have had on a bad day. Quit everything. Move to a cabin in the mountains. No inbox, no traffic, no difficult relatives, just silence and snow. In Nanak's time, some people really did it. High in the Himalayas lived the sidhs, yogis who had left the world behind for caves and peaks, and who were said to have mastered the body and the mind. On his journey north, tradition says, Nanak climbed up to meet them. And they were curious about him. Here was a man clearly on a spiritual path, singing about God, and yet he had a wife, children, a home in the plains, and he kept going back to it. Today, the question they asked.
screen: `THE CABIN-IN-THE-MOUNTAINS FANTASY.` → `YOGIS WHO REALLY LEFT.` → `A VISITOR WITH A FAMILY.`

segments.voice: Sidh means one who has succeeded, someone who has reached the goal, a perfected one. These yogis wore earrings and ash and carried begging bowls, and they believed that to find the truth you had to leave ordinary life. Bhai Gurdas tells a version of the meeting in his verses. The yogis ask Nanak how things are going down in the world. And he answers, sharply, that the world is in darkness, because the people who should be lighting it have gone off to hide in the mountains. There's also a long conversation between Nanak and the yogis in the scripture itself, called the Sidh Gosht, the talk with the sidhs, in raga Ramkali. They ask him question after question, and one answer is the heart of this day. How do you live in the world? Like a lotus, he says, which grows in the water but floats clean on top of it. Like a duck, which swims in the stream and comes out dry. You don't have to leave the water. You just don't let it soak in. That's the Sikh ideal in one picture, and it goes right back to Nanak. Not the monk, not the hermit, but the householder: someone who works, raises a family, pays the bills, and keeps God in mind the whole time, unstained by greed and ego. Sikhs don't look down on the yogis' devotion; Nanak spoke with them for hours. But his answer was a different path. Stay. Work. Love your people. And float.
screen: `SIDH — ONE WHO HAS SUCCEEDED.` · `WHO LIGHTS THE WORLD, IF YOU HIDE?` · `LIKE A LOTUS, LIKE A DUCK.` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER'S PATH.` · then, large: `IN THE WORLD, UNSTAINED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one ordinary chore with care. The dishes, folding laundry, wiping a counter. For now, settle and choose it, and if you can, begin it while the bell runs. Do it slowly. Feel the water, the cloth, the weight of the plate. Let your mind stay with your hands. This is the lotus: right in the middle of ordinary life, and clean. The bell holds the time.
Sidh. A perfected one, the name for the yogis Nanak met in the mountains, who asked why he stayed in the world. Today's word.
Your line: in the world, unstained. Today, in the busiest moment, picture the lotus on the water, and float for one breath. Day thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs follow the householder's path Guru Nanak taught, working and raising families rather than renouncing the world; the Sidh Gosht, his dialogue with the yogis, is part of the Guru Granth Sahib and is studied and sung.

fork.setup: you're Nanak, high in the mountains. the yogis ask why you, a holy man, keep going back to your family and the world below. what do you answer?
options: you're right; I'll stay up here.
live in the world like a lotus in water.
the world is fine; there's nothing to worry about.
fork.reveal: in the Sidh Gosht, he answers with the lotus that floats clean on the water, and the duck that swims and stays dry.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sidh, from Sanskrit siddha, one who has succeeded, a perfected yogi.

trapdoor: what you thought: some yogis Nanak met on a hike.
what it means: the question of whether to leave the world, and Nanak's answer: stay in it, unstained, like a lotus on the water.
what a scholar hears: siddha, the perfected one; the Sidh Gosht in Ramkali, around Ang 938, is a full dialogue with Nath yogis, and the lotus and duck are its images.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ramkali, Sidh Gosht, Ang 938 (the lotus and the duck)
Bhai Gurdas, Var 1 (the meeting with the sidhs on the mountain)

notes: Sidh Gosht begins at Ang 938; the lotus/duck verse (jaise jal meh kamal niraalam, murgaaee nai saane) is at Ang 938. Confirm.
Bhai Gurdas Var 1 (around pauris 28–31) tells the Sumer mountain meeting and the 'world in darkness' reply; paraphrased. Confirm pauri and phrasing.
Whether the Sidh Gosht records the Himalayan meeting or a later one (tradition also places a debate at Achal Batala) is debated; script keeps them loosely together. Confirm.
Yogis identified as Nath/Siddha yogis with earrings and ash; confirm description.
